title: Systems of Linear Equations
summary: Solving Ax=b, Gaussian elimination, and rank — the machinery that connects straight to least squares and graphics transforms.

slides.markdown:
**Ax = b** is the central problem of linear algebra: given a matrix `A` and target vector `b`, find the vector `x` that makes it true.

Every "solve for the unknowns" problem — circuit equations, fitting a line, balancing a spreadsheet model — reduces to this form.

- `A` encodes the constraints/coefficients, `b` the targets, `x` the unknowns you're solving for.
- The system can have exactly one solution, none, or infinitely many.
- Gaussian elimination is the mechanical process that finds out which, and solves it.

slides.subTitle: Gaussian elimination
slides.markdown:
**Gaussian elimination** turns the augmented matrix `[A|b]` into row echelon form: use row operations (swap rows, scale a row, subtract a multiple of one row from another) to zero out everything below each pivot.

Once triangular, solve bottom-up by **back-substitution** — the last row gives one variable directly, then substitute upward.

![Gaussian elimination reducing a system to row echelon form](assets/gaussian-elimination-steps.svg)

slides.subTitle: Row echelon form and rank
slides.markdown:
The **rank** of a matrix is the number of linearly independent rows (equivalently columns) it has — the number of pivots you get after elimination.

Rank tells you how much genuine information the system carries. A `3x3` matrix with rank 2 means one equation is redundant — a combination of the other two, adding no new constraint.

Rank is the single number that predicts whether `Ax=b` has a unique solution, before you even finish solving it.

slides.subTitle: No solution, one, or infinitely many
slides.markdown:
After elimination, read the outcome straight off the reduced matrix:

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Full rank, square | Exactly one solution | `2x=4` -> `x=2` |
| Rank < unknowns | Infinitely many solutions | `x+y=4` -> a whole line of answers |
| A row reduces to `0 = c` (c≠0) | No solution — contradiction | `x+y=2` and `x+y=5` at once |

Decide by finishing elimination first: the row pattern, not intuition, tells you which case you're in.

slides.subTitle: Least squares — the practical case
slides.markdown:
Real data usually gives you an **overdetermined** system: more equations (data points) than unknowns (parameters), and no exact solution exists — the data is noisy.

Instead of solving `Ax=b` exactly, **least squares** finds the `x` that minimizes how wrong the equations are overall: `min ||Ax - b||²`.

This is the single most common real use of "solving a linear system" — fitting any linear model to noisy, real-world data.

slides.subTitle: Least squares intuition
slides.markdown:
Least squares picks the `x` minimizing the **sum of squared errors** between predictions `Ax` and actual `b`. Squaring does two things: it makes all errors positive (no cancellation), and it penalizes large errors disproportionately more than small ones.

The solution comes from setting the gradient of that squared error to zero, giving the **normal equations** `AᵀAx = Aᵀb`.

This is exactly the mechanics behind fitting linear regression (Area 12 `supervised-learning`) — regression *is* least squares applied to a features matrix.

slides.subTitle: Ill-conditioned systems
slides.markdown:
A system is **ill-conditioned** when tiny changes in `A` or `b` cause huge swings in the solution `x` — even though the math is technically solvable.

This happens when rows/columns of `A` are nearly (not exactly) linearly dependent — near-collinear features, or near-parallel constraint lines that barely intersect.

The practical symptom: your "exact" solver returns wildly different answers for barely-different input data. The fix isn't a better solver — it's regularization or removing the near-redundant dimension.
